Trying to Conceive

What to Eat When Trying to Get Pregnant: Fertility Nutrition

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When you are trying to get pregnant, the most helpful way to eat is an overall pattern built on vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts, low-mercury fish, and unsaturated fats like olive oil, rather than any single fertility food. Research links this kind of pattern with better fertility outcomes, though food is one factor among many and no diet can guarantee a pregnancy. This guide walks through the nutrients that matter most before conception, where to find them in ordinary groceries, and which popular fertility foods you can safely ignore.

Start with the pattern, not a superfood

There is no single food that has been proven to make pregnancy happen. What researchers have found, mostly in large observational studies, is that people who eat a pattern rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish, and unsaturated fats tend to have better fertility outcomes than people who eat mostly refined carbohydrates, processed meat, and added sugar. This kind of research shows associations, not guarantees, and diet is only one of many factors. Still, it points in a consistent and reassuring direction: the same everyday eating pattern that supports your heart and general health also supports your reproductive health.

In practice, that means thinking in swaps rather than rules. Choose whole grains like oats, brown rice, or whole wheat bread over white versions most of the time. Cook with olive or canola oil instead of relying on butter or heavily processed fats. Let beans, lentils, nuts, and fish take turns with meat across the week. Keep fruit and vegetables where you can actually see them, because visible food gets eaten. None of this needs to be perfect, and one takeout night changes nothing. You are building a background pattern, and background patterns are judged over months, not single meals.

Folate and iron come first

Folate is the nutrient with the clearest before-pregnancy job: it helps the neural tube form and close within about the first month after conception, often before most people know they are pregnant. Food sources include leafy greens such as spinach and romaine, beans and lentils, oranges, avocado, and fortified breads and cereals, which use a form called folic acid. Because the timing matters so much, health authorities such as the CDC recommend that anyone who could become pregnant take folic acid daily in addition to eating folate-rich foods. The exact dose and when to start are covered in our folic acid guide, so treat this page as the food half of the plan.

Iron deserves attention because pregnancy raises your blood volume and iron needs quickly, and starting with low stores makes early pregnancy harder. Some research also links iron from plant foods with better ovulatory function. Good sources include lean beef, poultry, eggs, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, pumpkin seeds, and fortified cereals. Your body absorbs plant iron better when you pair it with vitamin C, so add peppers, citrus, tomatoes, or berries to the same meal. Heavy periods, a vegetarian or vegan diet, or a history of anemia are all good reasons to ask a clinician about checking your iron before you conceive rather than after.

Fish and omega-3s without the mercury worry

Fish is one of the most useful fertility foods because it delivers protein, omega-3 fats, vitamin D, and iodine in one package. The FDA and EPA advise that people who are pregnant or may become pregnant eat 2 to 3 servings of low-mercury fish per week, which works out to about 8 to 12 ounces in total. Salmon, sardines, trout, herring, anchovies, shrimp, tilapia, and canned light tuna all fit. The fish to skip are the large, long-lived predators that concentrate mercury: shark, swordfish, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico, and bigeye tuna.

If you do not eat fish, you can still get omega-3 building blocks from walnuts, chia seeds, ground flaxseed, and canola oil, though the plant form converts to the long-chain fats less efficiently. An algae-based omega-3 supplement is another option worth raising with a clinician or pharmacist, and our prenatal vitamin guide covers how supplements fit together. Frozen and canned fish count just as much as fresh, and they are usually cheaper. A simple habit like canned salmon on toast or a weekly frozen fillet gets you most of the benefit without turning dinner into a project.

Vitamin D, iodine, and calcium

Vitamin D supports bone health and plays a role in hormone function, and low levels are common, especially in northern climates and through the winter. Food sources are limited but real: fatty fish, egg yolks, fortified milk and plant milks, and fortified cereals. Iodine matters because your thyroid uses it to make the hormones that help regulate ovulation and, later, fetal brain development. Iodized table salt, dairy, eggs, and seafood are the main sources, and people who cook only with specialty salts like sea salt or kosher salt often get less than they think. Neither nutrient requires an exotic food, just a check that your regular staples include them.

Calcium keeps your own bones protected once pregnancy begins drawing on your stores. Dairy products, fortified plant milks, tofu set with calcium, canned fish with soft bones, and leafy greens like kale all contribute. Full-fat and low-fat dairy are both reasonable choices, so pick what you enjoy and can afford. If your diet excludes whole food groups, if you have had bariatric surgery, or if you follow a vegan diet, a clinician or dietitian can help you spot gaps before you conceive. For which supplements are worth taking and when to start them, see our guides on prenatal vitamins and folic acid rather than adding products one by one.

Body weight, cycles, and the myths you can skip

Body weight can influence fertility mainly through its effect on ovulation. Weight at either end of the range, significantly low or significantly high, can make cycles irregular or pause ovulation altogether, and organizations like ACOG note that even modest changes toward a comfortable middle can help cycles return to a steadier rhythm. This is not about reaching a perfect number, and weight is only one factor among many. If your periods are irregular, very light, or absent, mention it to a clinician early rather than assuming diet alone will fix it. The same goes for time: if you are under 35 and have been trying for a year, or 35 or older and trying for six months, book a fertility evaluation no matter how well you eat. Tracking your cycles, along with any changes you make, in the BeMama app can make that conversation faster and more concrete.

A few myths deserve a plain answer. There is no good evidence that pineapple core helps implantation; the enzyme it contains is digested like any other protein. Fertility teas and detox blends are not tested for effectiveness or pregnancy safety, and some herbs are better avoided while trying. No single superfood, from maca to royal jelly, has solid evidence behind it, and expensive powders mostly buy hope. Full-fat dairy shows a possible link with ovulation in some research, but it is a candidate, not a prescription. When a product promises to boost fertility fast, treat that as a signal to keep your money and put it toward groceries instead.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fertility is influenced by many factors, and no food, supplement, timing trick, or lifestyle routine guarantees conception. A varied eating pattern, appropriate activity, avoiding smoking and drugs, and reviewing alcohol, medicines, and workplace exposures support general preconception health for both partners.

Male fertility can also be affected by age, smoking, heavy alcohol or drug use, certain medicines and treatments, heat exposure, and health conditions. Persistent concerns deserve medical assessment rather than increasingly restrictive diets or unproven supplements.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note meals, habits, supplements, and questions you want to discuss. The app does not score fertility, semen quality, or whether a particular diet increases the chance of pregnancy.

When to seek help

Check supplements and major diet changes with a healthcare professional, especially when you take medicine or have a medical condition.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • No single food boosts fertility; the overall pattern of your diet is what matters.
  • Build most meals around vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish, and unsaturated fats.
  • Folate and iron are the two nutrients to prioritize from food before conception.
  • Aim for 2 to 3 servings of low-mercury fish per week, about 8 to 12 ounces in total.
  • Skip fertility teas and superfoods, and ask a clinician early about irregular cycles.

Frequently asked questions

Does diet affect fertility?

Yes, diet appears to affect fertility, though it is one factor among many. Large observational studies link eating patterns rich in vegetables, whole grains, legumes, fish, and unsaturated fats with better fertility outcomes. That research shows associations rather than guarantees, so think of food as improving the odds, not controlling the result.

What are the best foods for fertility?

The best foods for fertility are ordinary ones: leafy greens, beans and lentils, whole grains, nuts, fruit, eggs, dairy, and low-mercury fish like salmon and sardines. Together they cover folate, iron, omega-3 fats, vitamin D, iodine, and calcium. No exotic ingredient outperforms a consistent pattern built from these staples.

Are there foods that increase fertility on their own?

No single food has been shown to increase fertility on its own. Claims about pineapple core, maca, royal jelly, and fertility teas are not backed by solid evidence, and some herbal blends lack safety data for early pregnancy. Your overall eating pattern over weeks and months is what the research actually supports.

Is there a specific fertility diet I should follow?

There is no official fertility diet, and you do not need a named plan to eat well for conception. Patterns close to a Mediterranean style, with plenty of plants, whole grains, fish, and olive oil, keep showing up in fertility research, so use that as a loose template. If you have a condition like PCOS, diabetes, or celiac disease, ask your clinician or a dietitian for advice tailored to you.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
